title: Classical Additive STDP
intro: The foundational timing rule. A presynaptic spike shortly before a postsynaptic spike strengthens the synapse, the reverse order weakens it, and the effect fades exponentially with the gap.

blocks.text: Let Δt = t_post − t_pre. In additive STDP the weight change for one pair depends only on Δt, not on the current weight:

blocks.source:
Δw = A₊ · exp(−Δt / τ₊)     if Δt > 0   (pre before post: LTP)
Δw = −A₋ · exp( Δt / τ₋)     if Δt < 0   (post before pre: LTD)
w  ← clip(w + Δw, 0, w_max)

typical: τ₊ ≈ τ₋ ≈ 20 ms,  A₋·τ₋ slightly larger than A₊·τ₊

blocks.text: Bi and Poo measured the window in cultured hippocampal neurons, and Markram and colleagues in neocortical slices. Song, Miller and Abbott then showed what the rule does in a network: synapses compete. Inputs that reliably precede the postsynaptic spike win, the rest are driven to zero, and the neuron's firing rate is regulated without any explicit normalisation.

The curve is the change caused by a single pre-post pair. The area of the right lobe (A₊τ₊) against the left lobe (A₋τ₋) decides what uncorrelated input does: if LTD dominates, random pairings weaken synapses on average, which keeps the total input bounded.

For Poisson inputs uncorrelated with the output, the expected drift is proportional to A₊τ₊ − A₋τ₋. If it is positive, every synapse grows until it hits w_max and the neuron saturates. A small negative bias makes uncorrelated synapses decay, while correlated ones, which get extra causal pairings, still grow. Song et al. used A₋/A₊ ≈ 1.05 with equal time constants.

items: All-to-all: every pre spike pairs with every post spike. This is the trace implementation where traces add.
Nearest-neighbour: each spike pairs only with the most recent spike of the other neuron (traces reset to 1 instead of adding). This changes the behaviour at high rates.
Above about 10 Hz, the choice of pairing scheme matters as much as the window shape.
Bimodal weights: with hard bounds, weights pile up at 0 and at w_max. That gives sharp selectivity but loses graded information.
Learns latency: neurons become sensitive to the earliest reliable inputs, so repeated spatiotemporal patterns are detected faster with practice (Masquelier & Thorpe 2007).
No frequency effects: at high pairing rates real synapses potentiate even for post-before-pre order. Capturing that needs triplet or voltage rules.
Unstable alone: without inhibition or homeostasis, a whole layer tends to learn the same feature.

blocks.text: For a cortical column: classical STDP plus winner-take-all lateral inhibition is the standard recipe for unsupervised feature learning in a spiking layer (Diehl & Cook 2015 learned MNIST digits this way). In a column model it is a good first rule for the feedforward synapses into layer 4, with an adaptive threshold per neuron so that different neurons claim different features.

Sources: Bi & Poo (1998) J Neurosci 18:10464; Markram, Lübke, Frotscher & Sakmann (1997) Science 275:213; Song, Miller & Abbott (2000) Nat Neurosci 3:919; Masquelier & Thorpe (2007) Unsupervised learning of visual features through spike timing dependent plasticity, PLoS Comput Biol 3; Diehl & Cook (2015) Unsupervised learning of digit recognition using spike-timing-dependent plasticity, Front Comput Neurosci 9; Gerstner et al., Neuronal Dynamics (2014), ch. 19.
